notes.h: Background: partition, the Crown link and the 1948 government
notes.b: Anglo-Irish relations after 1949 grew out of how Ireland had been divided and how the South's links with Britain were loosened. These background facts explain why a declaration of a republic in 1949 caused such a reaction in London and Belfast.
points: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 set up Northern Ireland with its own parliament at Stormont (in Belfast). The Irish Free State followed in 1922, so the island was divided into two states.

A unionist majority (people who wanted Northern Ireland to stay in the United Kingdom) governed the North, and nationalists (who wanted Irish unity) were a large minority there. This is why partition stayed a live dispute.
The External Relations Act of 1936 left the Crown with a role in Irish external affairs, so Ireland was still linked to the British monarch for diplomatic purposes.
The 1937 Constitution (Bunreacht na hÉireann) claimed the whole island in Articles 2 and 3, which set the Irish state's official position against partition.

The First Inter-Party Government of 1948 to 1951 took office in February 1948 under John A. Costello as Taoiseach, with Seán MacBride of Clann na Poblachta as Minister for External Affairs, and moved to declare a republic.
Ireland was neutral in the Second World War and did not join NATO. Even so, Britain, Northern Ireland and the Republic stayed closely linked by trade, migration and sterling (the British currency).
notes.tip: A short, dated account of this background helps you place any source on partition or on the 1949 acts in its context.

notes.h: The Republic of Ireland Act and the Ireland Act, 1949
notes.b: The declaration of a republic completed the separation from Britain in the South but hardened partition in British law. Britain's reply, the Ireland Act, is the starting point for the whole story.
points: Costello announced the repeal of the External Relations Act while in Canada (Ottawa) in September 1948. The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force on 18 April 1949 (Easter Monday).
That Irish Act ended the Crown link under the External Relations Act, and Ireland formally left the Commonwealth because a republic could no longer share a monarch with the other members.

Britain responded with the Ireland Act 1949. It declared that the Republic was not a foreign country for British law and that Irish citizens in Britain were not treated as aliens, so they kept their rights, including to vote, work and receive benefits.
The Act also stated that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, which gave unionists a veto over any change.
The Irish government saw the Ireland Act as a guarantee of partition and a betrayal of nationalists.
The Common Travel Area, which allowed free movement between the two islands, continued after 1949. This mattered to the large number of Irish emigrants living in Britain.
Articles 2 and 3 of the 1937 Constitution claimed the whole island as the national territory. Unionists and the British government cited them as proof that Dublin did not accept Northern Ireland.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two acts: the Republic of Ireland Act is Irish (passed 1948, in force April 1949) and the Ireland Act is British (1949). For a paragraph, give the two provisions of the Ireland Act, the consent guarantee and the dates.

notes.b: In the years after 1949 Irish governments tried to end partition by publicity and diplomacy. When that failed, the IRA turned to force, and by the late 1950s the Irish state changed course.
points: The 1948 to 1951 government launched an anti-partition campaign with the support of all the main parties, aiming to win international sympathy for Irish unity.
Irish ministers spoke abroad, especially in the United States, and complained that nationalists in Northern Ireland were treated unfairly.
Britain and the unionist government at Stormont refused to discuss the question, so the campaign produced no practical gain.
The IRA's Border Campaign ran from December 1956 to 1962. It had little support in the Republic, and the Irish government interned (jailed without trial) suspects at the Curragh from 1957 to 1959.
By the late 1950s Irish governments moved to a more pragmatic, economic approach and concentrated on economic recovery, because rhetoric about partition had achieved nothing.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the cause behind each shift. Here the cause of the move away from anti-partition rhetoric is its failure and the need for economic recovery.

notes.b: Ireland's economy was tied to Britain's, and this shaped how far Irish governments could afford to quarrel with London. It explains much of the move to cooperation from the 1960s.
points: In the late 1950s about 70 to 75 per cent of Irish exports, mainly live cattle and other farm produce, went to Britain, so Irish farmers depended on the British market.

Britain was also the main source of imports. The Irish pound was tied to sterling until Ireland joined the European Monetary System in 1979, so Irish prices and interest rates followed British conditions.

This dependence is why Irish policy-makers sought to join the EEC (the European Economic Community, forerunner of the European Union) only when Britain did, and why the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement of 1965 mattered.

Both countries joined the EEC in 1973, and Ireland joined the European Monetary System in 1979 while Britain stayed out. The share of exports going to Britain then fell steadily, to under half by the early 1980s.
notes.tip: Trade dependence is the stated cause of the move to cooperation in 1965. Quote the range 'about 70 to 75 per cent' for the late 1950s rather than a single figure.

notes.h: Lemass, O'Neill and the Free Trade Agreement, 1965
notes.b: In 1965 relations between Dublin, Belfast and London became more cooperative than at any time since partition.
points: Seán Lemass, the Taoiseach, went to Stormont on 14 January 1965 and met Terence O'Neill, the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. The visit was arranged in secret. O'Neill then visited Dublin on 9 February 1965.
These were the first meetings between the heads of government of the two parts of Ireland since partition, and the agenda was trade, tourism and electricity rather than partition.

Lemass accepted the North's existence in practice and talked of cooperation, which marked a change from the anti-partition rhetoric of the 1950s. The Irish government's declaration on consent came later, in 1973 and 1985.
Ian Paisley and other unionists protested at the meetings, and some in O'Neill's own party mistrusted them.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed on 14 December 1965. Tariff cuts began in 1966 and were phased in over a number of years, so trade between Ireland and Britain became freer gradually.
notes.tip: For a paragraph, say who met whom, where, when and what they discussed. Keep the dates apart: Lemass at Stormont is 14 January, O'Neill in Dublin is 9 February, and the Free Trade Agreement is December 1965.

notes.b: Violence in Northern Ireland from 1969 tested relations between the Irish and British governments, and Jack Lynch, the Taoiseach, had to balance public feeling in the South against the need to keep working with London. Each crisis produced a response from Dublin that you should be able to date.
points: After rioting in Derry and Belfast in August 1969, Lynch said in a broadcast on 13 August that the Irish government could no longer stand by. He refused to send troops across the border, and the British army was deployed on the streets on 14 August 1969.
Ireland raised the crisis at the United Nations in August 1969 without result. On 4 September 1969 Patrick Hillery, the Minister for External Affairs, visited the Falls Road in Belfast.

The Arms Crisis of May 1970, when Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney on 6 May, showed the division inside Fianna Fáil over how to respond to the North. There is more on this in the notes on the economic and social challenges of the 1970s and 1980s.

In September 1971 Lynch met Edward Heath, the British Prime Minister, and Brian Faulkner, the Northern Ireland Prime Minister, at Chequers. Lynch argued that an Irish dimension (a role for Dublin) was needed to end the violence.

Internment (jailing suspects without trial) was introduced on 9 August 1971 and condemned by the Irish government. Ireland took the United Kingdom to the European Commission and Court of Human Rights, and in January 1978 the Court found that the interrogation techniques used were inhuman and degrading treatment (not torture).

On Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, soldiers of the Parachute Regiment shot dead thirteen people at a civil rights march in Derry, and a fourteenth died later. The Irish ambassador in London was recalled and 2 February 1972 was a day of mourning in the Republic.

Later judgements on Bloody Sunday differed. The Widgery Report of April 1972 was widely seen as a whitewash, but the Saville Inquiry report of June 2010 found the killings unjustified, and David Cameron apologised.

On 2 February 1972 a crowd burned the British embassy in Merrion Square, Dublin, and the British government protested. In March 1972 Heath suspended Stormont and introduced direct rule from Westminster, which Dublin welcomed as a step towards a new settlement.
notes.tip: Ordinary-level answers must tie each fact to what Lynch did: refused to send troops, the Arms Crisis, the reaction to internment and Bloody Sunday (ambassador recalled), and Chequers. Keep internment (9 August 1971), Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) and the embassy burning (2 February 1972) in order.

notes.h: Joint EEC entry and the Sunningdale Agreement, 1973–1974
notes.b: In 1973 Britain and Ireland entered the EEC together and the two governments, with Northern Ireland's moderate parties, tried to agree a settlement. It failed within months, and security strains continued afterwards.
points: Ireland and Britain, with Denmark, joined the EEC on 1 January 1973. Their ministers began to meet regularly in Brussels, which improved personal contacts between the two governments.
Liam Cosgrave led a Fine Gael-Labour coalition from March 1973, with Garret FitzGerald as Minister for Foreign Affairs from 1973 to 1977.

The Sunningdale Agreement of December 1973 (agreed at a conference at Sunningdale, Berkshire) involved Heath for the British government and Cosgrave for the Irish government. The Northern parties were the Ulster Unionists under Faulkner, the SDLP under Gerry Fitt and the Alliance Party under Oliver Napier.

It provided for a power-sharing executive (unionists and nationalists governing together), with Faulkner as chief executive and Fitt as deputy, and a Council of Ireland to give the Republic a say in North-South cooperation.

The Irish government declared that there would be no change in the status of Northern Ireland until a majority there wished it. This did not end the constitutional claim, because Articles 2 and 3 stayed until 1998.

Loyalists opposed the Council of Ireland because it gave Dublin a role in the North. The Ulster Workers' Council strike, from 15 to 28 May 1974, ended the executive, so Sunningdale collapsed within about five months.
On 17 May 1974, during the strike, car bombs in Dublin and Monaghan killed 33 people. They were attributed to loyalists and no one was convicted.

The IRA killed Christopher Ewart-Biggs, the British ambassador to Ireland, near Dublin on 21 July 1976. A state of emergency was declared and further emergency legislation followed in 1976, which shows the security strain of the mid-1970s.
notes.tip: Be able to state who took part at Sunningdale, what was agreed, and why it ran into opposition and failed in months. Do not confuse Sunningdale (1973, Heath and Cosgrave) with the Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985, Thatcher and FitzGerald).

notes.b: Relations moved from security cooperation after IRA attacks in 1979 to a promising summit in 1980 and then a rift in 1982. Charles Haughey and Margaret Thatcher were very different leaders, and a quarrel over the Falklands War ended their dialogue.
points: On 27 August 1979 the IRA killed Lord Mountbatten at Mullaghmore, Co. Sligo. The same day eighteen British soldiers were killed at Warrenpoint, Co. Down. Lynch met Thatcher in September 1979 and security cooperation was agreed.
Thatcher became Prime Minister in May 1979 and Haughey became Taoiseach on 11 December 1979. Haughey met her in London in May 1980 and in Dublin on 8 December 1980.

The Dublin summit's joint communique spoke of studies of 'the totality of relationships within these islands'. Haughey presented this as a breakthrough, but Thatcher said constitutional status was not in question, so the two leaders read it differently.
The 1981 hunger strikes, in which ten republican prisoners died, including Bobby Sands on 5 May 1981, strained relations between the two governments.
In November 1981 Thatcher and FitzGerald, by then Taoiseach, set up the Anglo-Irish Intergovernmental Council. Do not confuse it with the Haughey-Thatcher summit of December 1980.

In the Falklands War (April to June 1982) Ireland, then a member of the UN Security Council, at first supported EEC sanctions on Argentina. After the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was sunk on 2 May 1982, Haughey's government withdrew its support in early May and called for a ceasefire.
Thatcher was angered and saw the withdrawal as a breach of solidarity, and trust between the two leaders did not recover while Haughey was in office.

The dispute set Irish neutrality (staying out of other countries' wars) against solidarity with Britain as a fellow EEC member. Haughey's government acted on the first, while Thatcher judged by the second.
notes.tip: Strong essays compare Haughey's 1980 dialogue and its collapse over the Falklands with FitzGerald's Forum and the 1985 agreement, naming what each achieved and failed to achieve. Say that the Falklands caused the rift.

notes.h: FitzGerald, the New Ireland Forum and the Anglo-Irish Agreement, 1983–1985
notes.b: Garret FitzGerald built on the Forum to reach the main achievement of Anglo-Irish diplomacy in this period, the agreement signed at Hillsborough. It gave Dublin a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs without granting it authority.
points: The New Ireland Forum opened in Dublin Castle on 30 May 1983 and reported on 2 May 1984. It brought together Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP.
Its report offered three options: a unitary state (the preferred option), a federal or confederal state, and joint authority (shared British and Irish rule).
Thatcher publicly rejected all three at a press conference on 19 November 1984 ('out, out, out'). Even so, the Forum had strengthened the SDLP and shown that nationalists had a common position.
Negotiations between officials followed, and FitzGerald and Thatcher signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement at Hillsborough Castle, Co. Down, on 15 November 1985.

Both governments affirmed the consent principle: the status of Northern Ireland would change only with the consent of a majority there. The Intergovernmental Conference was co-chaired by the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and the Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, with a secretariat at Maryfield, near Belfast.
The Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland affairs through the Conference, but it could not exercise authority, so this was a consultative role and not joint authority.
Unionists protested strongly. A huge rally at Belfast City Hall in November 1985 was followed by the resignation of fifteen unionist MPs in January 1986 to force by-elections.

Fianna Fáil under Haughey opposed the agreement. Desmond O'Malley had been expelled from Fianna Fáil in February 1985 over a vote on family planning law. He and Mary Harney founded the Progressive Democrats in December 1985, in opposition to Haughey's leadership.
notes.tip: Learn the signing date and place (15 November 1985, Hillsborough), the three Forum options and Thatcher's rejection. Naming both the unionist and the nationalist reactions to 1985 is rewarded.

notes.h: Why Thatcher signed, and how the agreement was read
notes.b: The agreement drew on motives from both governments, and nationalists and unionists drew opposite conclusions from it. These contrasting reactions are what examiners ask you to name.
points: Thatcher accepted the agreement partly for security reasons, because she wanted closer cooperation with Dublin against the IRA.
She also hoped that a role for Dublin would strengthen the SDLP, the nationalist party that rejected violence, against Sinn Féin.
Contemporary nationalists saw the agreement as recognition of their rights and of Dublin's concern for them.
Contemporary unionists saw it as a betrayal and a threat to the union, because it was made without their consent, which is why they protested and later boycotted the Conference.
notes.tip: Be able to state why Britain signed (security cooperation and support for the SDLP) and why the agreement survived while Sunningdale failed in months.

notes.b: By 1989 relations were far closer than in 1949, although the basic dispute over Northern Ireland remained unresolved. The agreement had survived and changed how the two governments dealt with each other.
points: The Intergovernmental Conference met regularly and cooperation on security and cross-border matters had grown, although unionists continued to boycott it.

Friction continued over extradition (handing suspects to the other state), over alleged miscarriages of justice affecting Irish people in British courts, and over the British army's conduct in Northern Ireland.
The IRA's campaign continued, and the North remained divided and violent.
Haughey had opposed the agreement in 1985, but he left it in place when Fianna Fáil formed a coalition with the Progressive Democrats in July 1989, after the general election of June 1989.
Joint EEC membership, the growth of North-South contacts and the habit of regular meetings meant that relations were closer than in 1949, even though the fundamental dispute remained.
notes.tip: A top essay on 1949 to 1989 argues a thesis, from bitterness over partition to regular cooperation, uses the dates 1949, 1965, 1972 to 1974, 1980 to 1982 and 1985, and judges how far relations improved.

notes.h: Assessment: partition, cooperation and the limits of agreement
notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement on how far Anglo-Irish relations improved. The evidence falls into paired points: what was achieved against what was not, and how contemporaries judged events against how historians judge them now.
points: Achievement: from the hostility of the Ireland Act in 1949, Ireland moved to regular contact with London and a formal consultative role in 1985.
Limit: Sunningdale collapsed within months, the 1985 agreement did not end the violence, and the two governments kept different aims.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw the Anglo-Irish Agreement as recognition of their rights.
Contemporary view: unionists saw it as betrayal, a threat to the union made without their consent.
Later view: historians see the agreement as a foundation for the Downing Street Declaration of December 1993 and the Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998, although its immediate effect was limited.
notes.tip: Achievements against limits and contemporary against later views earn credit as paired points. Name the cause behind each shift: the Ireland Act, trade dependence, violence in the North, joint EEC entry, the Falklands and the Forum.

keyTerms.definition: The British law that kept Northern Ireland in the United Kingdom unless its parliament consented, and treated the Republic as not a foreign country.
The Irish government's diplomatic and publicity effort of the late 1940s to win support for ending the division of the island.
The arrangement allowing Irish and British citizens to travel, live and work in each other's country without immigration controls.
The December 1973 agreement on a power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland and a Council of Ireland, which collapsed in May 1974.
The loyalist general strike of May 1974 that brought down the power-sharing executive.
The 1983 to 1984 meeting of nationalist parties that proposed three options for the future of Ireland, all rejected by Thatcher.
The November 1985 agreement giving the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland through an Intergovernmental Conference.
The phrase in the December 1980 Haughey-Thatcher communique about studying the relationship between the two islands as a whole.
The principle that the constitutional status of Northern Ireland would change only with the agreement of a majority of its people.
